source.title: Target-Aware Language Modeling via Granular Data Sampling
source.authors: Er-Nie Chang; Pin-Jie Lin; Yang Li; Changsheng Zhao; Daeil Kim; Rastislav Rabatin; Ze-Chun Liu; Yang-Yang Shi; Vikas Chandra

record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates downstream task performance across model sizes, which bears on V6, but does not fit or test the original scaling-law measurements.
record.gate_note: The study reports pretraining on sampled data and downstream benchmark scores. Its data-selection comparisons and tokenizer ablations are not results about scaling-law loss or compute-optimal allocation. Figure 3 is the reported result that bears on V6; its plotted scores are not provided as text values.
record.test_reason: The study is about data selection, not scaling. Incidentally, it trains four sizes (125M to 1.5B) on a fixed ~700M-token, 1% RefinedWeb sample and reports average zero-shot accuracy rising with size. That bears weakly on V6's 'improves with scale' part. No fit, extrapolation or loss-to-task mapping is reported, so the predictability part is untested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but it shifts the emphasis. The main conclusion is that importance sampling with multi-granular n-gram features selects ~1% of RefinedWeb and beats random and word n-gram selection across 125M to 1.5B models. The abstract also claims parity with full RefinedWeb, a result not shown. The authors mention in passing that performance improves with size, then plateaus, with an 'emergent' bump at 350M.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains models on selected data and evaluates downstream tasks; it does not use the original studies' held-out pretraining-loss measurements or compute-optimal allocation procedure.
record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The scaling-related result is an average over eight downstream tasks, shown in a plot without numerical values in the text. The study reports averaging over three initialization runs but gives no uncertainty estimates for this result. It does not measure held-out pretraining loss or test a scaling-law fit.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 and the appendix report downstream-task comparisons for multiple tasks, model sizes, and sampling methods. These were not extracted because they compare data-selection approaches rather than testing the scaling relationship in V6, and the flattened table presentation makes reliable row-to-score assignment difficult.

untested.parts: Quantitative predictability: no fitted curve, no extrapolation, and no relation of task scores to pretraining loss. Only 4 sizes are tested, with token count fixed.

missing.what: Per-size AVG values for each selection method are in Table 1 but the rows record them as figure-only. The flattened text appears to give Random 45.59/49.56/50.61/51.49, N-gram 46.27/51.52/52.13/54.26 and Multi-granular 47.59/51.61/52.42/54.53 for 125M/350M/500M/1.5B. Per-task scores by size are also available.

record.verdict_notes: The plateau the authors note occurs with tokens fixed at ~700M for every size. Larger models are therefore data-bottlenecked, so the plateau is not evidence against V6 and I gave no limits_scope label. The authors' word 'emergent' at 350M rests on four points with no fit. No uncertainty is reported despite three seeds. Table 1 is flattened, so the column-to-value assignment is a best reading and should be checked against the PDF.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameter count, tokens, or compute.
Whether power-law fits from smaller runs predict larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocations and their trends with compute.
Effects of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities, repeated-data settings, fine-tuning, or transfer.
The study reports downstream scores across sizes, but does not test their quantitative predictability from pretraining loss or a fitted scaling law.
Dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits on setup or fitting choices, and departures from single power laws.

relationships.condition: Decoder LMs from 125M to 1.5B trained on ~700M tokens of a 1% RefinedWeb sample, under Random, N-gram and Multi-granular selection; average of eight zero-shot tasks
relationships.reason: Averages rise monotonically with size for all three selection methods (e.g. Random ≈45.6→51.5; r2-r4, r6-r8, r10-r12 vs r1, r5, r9). Values are read from flattened Table 1, and predictability is not tested.
relationships.display_finding: Average accuracy rises monotonically with size for all three selection methods, including approximately 45.6 to 51.5 with random selection, without testing predictive extrapolation.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
